title: Result day: a portal that survives the rush

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own result-day design case, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

scenario: A state university publishes semester results for **12 lakh students** at 10:00 am on a fixed day. Every year the old portal crashes within minutes, students refresh in panic, and the story makes the news. Design a results portal that stays up on result day: a student enters a roll number and date of birth and sees the marksheet, which can be downloaded as a PDF.

clarifying_questions.q: How many students, and how many look at results in the first hour?
clarifying_questions.a: 12 lakh students; assume 80% check within the first hour, many of them several times.
Rarely: re-evaluation corrections over the following weeks. On result day they are fixed.
No accounts: roll number plus date of birth is the check.
About 10 subjects with marks and grades, totals, SGPA; about 2 KB as JSON, about 60 KB as a PDF.
The exam cell's database computes them the night before; the portal only reads.

clarifying_questions.q: Is a delay of a few seconds acceptable at 10:00?
clarifying_questions.a: Yes, but pages must load in under a second once open, and no error pages.

functional: Look up a result by roll number and date of birth
Show the marksheet and offer a PDF download
Refuse wrong roll number or date of birth without saying which part was wrong
Publish all results at one moment, not before

non_functional.name: Peak load
non_functional.target: about 1,000 lookups per second sustained, bursts of 5,000

non_functional.name: Latency
non_functional.target: p99 under 300 ms for the marksheet page

non_functional.name: Correctness
non_functional.target: no student ever sees another student's result

estimates.question: Peak lookups per second if 12 lakh students check in the first hour, each 3 times on average, and the first 10 minutes carry 40% of the hour?
Size of all marksheets as JSON at 2 KB each, in megabytes?
estimates.working: 12,00,000 × 2 KB = 24,00,000 KB ≈ 2,400 MB: small enough to sit entirely in a cache.

estimates.question: Outgoing bandwidth in megabits per second if 30% of peak lookups (1,920 per second) also download a 60 KB PDF?

expected_components.name: CDN in front of everything
expected_components.why: Serves the static page, scripts and pre-built PDFs from the edge so the origin sees only the lookups.

expected_components.name: Precomputed result store (key-value)
expected_components.why: Results are fixed on the day, so build one record per student the night before, keyed by a hash of roll number and date of birth.

expected_components.name: In-memory cache (Redis or similar) holding all results
expected_components.why: 2.4 GB fits in memory; every lookup becomes one cache read, never a database query.

expected_components.name: Stateless lookup service behind a load balancer
expected_components.why: Scales out horizontally for the burst; any server can answer any request.

expected_components.name: Rate limiting per IP and per roll number
expected_components.why: Stops scripted guessing of dates of birth and limits refresh storms.

expected_components.name: Object storage for pre-rendered PDFs
expected_components.why: PDFs are generated the night before and served through the CDN, so result day does no rendering.

expected_components.name: Publish switch (feature flag)
expected_components.why: Results are loaded hours early but invisible until 10:00; one flag flips for every server at once.

expected_components.name: Waiting room page
expected_components.why: If the burst exceeds capacity, a static queue page is better than errors.

api: GET /results/{token}.pdf → 302 to a signed CDN URL
data_model: results_kv: key = SHA-256(roll || dob || secret salt) → { roll, name, subjects: [{code, marks, grade}], total, sgpa, pdf_path }. The exam cell's relational database stays the source of truth; the key-value store is a read-only copy built per publication.

diagram.alt: Students reach a CDN; lookups go through a load balancer to stateless lookup servers that read an in-memory cache filled the night before from the exam cell database; PDFs come from object storage through the CDN.

deep_dives.topic: Why precompute instead of caching on demand
deep_dives.body: With cache-aside, the first request for each roll number misses and hits the database, and at 10:00 **every** request is a first request: the cache is cold exactly when the load peaks. Because results are fixed and small, we **warm the whole cache before publication**: one batch job writes 12 lakh records into the cache and builds the PDFs. On the day there are no misses, so the database never sees result-day traffic at all.

Roll numbers are sequential and dates of birth fall in a narrow range, so an attacker could try every date for a roll number (about 1,500 tries). Rate limits per roll number (say 10 failed tries per hour) and per IP stop this. The key is a salted hash, so even a leaked cache dump does not list roll numbers, and the error message never says whether the roll number or the date was wrong.

Loading results at 10:00 would itself be a spike. Instead the data is loaded at night behind a publish flag that every lookup server checks (cached for a few seconds). At 10:00 the flag flips; within seconds every server answers. If something is wrong, flipping it back hides results without a deploy.

trade_offs: Precomputing everything costs a night-time batch job but makes result day a pure cache read.
A salted hash key protects privacy but means support staff cannot browse the cache by roll number.
A waiting room adds friction but turns overload into a queue instead of errors.
failure_modes: A cache node fails: run replicas and let the lookup service fall back to a read replica of the result store, with strict rate limits.
Wrong results were published: flip the publish flag off, fix, rebuild the affected keys, flip it on.
The CDN serves a stale 'not published yet' page: give that page a very short TTL and purge it at 10:00.

rubric.criterion: Asks about scale, read-only nature and the publication moment before designing.
Estimates peak QPS, data size and bandwidth and uses them to choose components.
Designs a read path with no database on the hot path: CDN, precomputed cache, stateless servers.
Handles the 10:00 spike: warming, publish switch, waiting room or similar.
Protects results from guessing and leaks: rate limits, salted keys, careful errors.
Explains trade-offs clearly and in a sensible order (AI feedback, advice only).

concept_checks.stem: Why is cache-aside alone a poor fit at 10:00 on result day?
options: Every request is a first request, so the cache is cold exactly at the peak
Redis is slower than a database
concept_checks.explanation: The cache fills only on misses, and at the moment of publication nothing has been read yet.

concept_checks.stem: Peak lookups are about 1,920 per second and a cache read takes 1 ms on one connection. Roughly how many concurrent connections must the service keep busy?
concept_checks.explanation: By Little's law, concurrency = rate × time = 1,920 × 0.001 ≈ 2. Throughput, not concurrency, is the hard part.

concept_checks.stem: What stops someone from trying every date of birth for a known roll number?
options: Rate limiting failed lookups per roll number and per IP
concept_checks.explanation: Only limiting attempts makes guessing slow enough to be useless.

concept_checks.stem: Why use a publish flag instead of loading results at 10:00?
options: Loading at night avoids a write spike at the read peak, and the flag can be flipped back without a deploy
It is required by the CDN
concept_checks.explanation: Loading early and revealing at once separates the write work from the read peak.

follow_ups: Re-evaluation results arrive two weeks later for 3% of students: how do you update without a second spike?
The university wants an SMS when a result is published: how do you send 12 lakh SMS without blocking the portal?
How would you prove after the day that no student saw another student's marksheet?

revision_card.front: Result-day portal: the one idea that makes it survive the spike?
revision_card.back: Precompute and pre-warm: build every result (and PDF) the night before into an in-memory store and object storage behind a publish flag; on the day the hot path is CDN → stateless server → cache read, with rate limits.
